title: STOMATIN-DEFICIENT CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS WITH NEUROLOGIC DEFECTS
alt_titles: GLUT1 DEFICIENCY SYNDROME WITH PSEUDOHYPERKALEMIA AND HEMOLYSIS
CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS, STOMATIN-DEFICIENT, WITH MENTAL RETARDATION, SEIZURES, CATARACTS, AND MASSIVE HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene (138140) on chromosome 1p34.2.

checks.claim: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We now show that sdCHC is associated with mutations in SLC2A1 that cause both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak
checks.explanation: The abstract links sdCHC to mutations in SLC2A1.

checks.claim: The SLC2A1 gene is located on chromosome 1p34.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Glucose transporter 1 (glut1) deficiency syndromes (glut1DSs) result from mutations in SLC2A1, encoding glut1.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene name. The abstract does not state it.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects is a rare form of stomatocytosis. Its red cells leak cations, and the leak is greatest in the cold. It is associated with hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, and also with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder (Flatt et al., 2011). Fricke et al. (2004) suggested that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis, occurring together with a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly, probably defined a new haemato-neurologic syndrome. Flatt et al. (2011) showed that the disorder is a form of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome caused by mutation in SLC2A1.

checks.evidence_quote: stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC), a rare form of stomatocytosis
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: In stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects, red cells leak cations, and the leak is greatest in the cold.
checks.evidence_quote: a rare form of stomatocytosis associated with a cold-induced cation leak
checks.explanation: A cold-induced cation leak is the same as the red cells leaking cations most in the cold.

checks.explanation: The abstract lists two patients and two disorders, which means one patient had each.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) reported 2 patients whose red cell cation leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, so that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C. This is the phenotype known as cryohydrocytosis. The authors stated that these were the only 2 known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both patients had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly.

checks.evidence_quote: while two showed a minimum at around 20-25 degrees C, such that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C
checks.explanation: The paper describes this minimum for the passive leak to K+, not for the cation leak in general.

checks.claim: The red cells of the 2 patients reported by Fricke et al. (2004) were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, the phenotype known as cryohydrocytosis.

Seizures developed later, and developmental milestones were delayed. The infant also had periventricular calcification. Visual impairment resulted from both cataracts and retinal dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) found that the 28-kD component of the erythrocyte membrane band 7 proteins was decreased in their patient with cryohydrocytosis and in their patient with hereditary stomatocytosis. On 2-dimensional electrophoresis, one of the 2 proteins in this component (22 x 8) was completely absent, whereas the other (60 x 8) was present as usual. All band 7 proteins, including 22 x 8, were always present in normal subjects and in reticulocytosis controls.

checks.evidence_quote: The 28,000-dalton component was decreased in both patients with permeability disorders.
checks.explanation: 28,000 daltons is the same as 28 kD, and the abstract says it was decreased in both patients.

checks.claim: On 2-dimensional electrophoresis, Lande et al. (1982) found that band 7 protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in their patients with cryohydrocytosis and hereditary stomatocytosis.
checks.evidence_quote: In the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis, 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was detected as usual.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: On 2-dimensional electrophoresis, Lande et al. (1982) found that band 7 protein 60 x 8 was present as usual in their patients with cryohydrocytosis and hereditary stomatocytosis.
checks.evidence_quote: In the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis, 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was detected as usual.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) studied 4 new cases of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis and 1 previously reported case. Western blotting showed a deficiency of the 32-kD red cell membrane protein stomatin, and all cases had marked cation leaks at 37 degrees C. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was incomplete: some red cells were stomatin-positive, and all platelets and neutrophils were stomatin-positive.

checks.evidence_quote: Three new isolated cases and one new pedigree are described, and one previously reported case is expanded.

checks.claim: The red cells of the infant reported by Bawazir et al. (2012) lost potassium in a temperature-dependent manner.

paragraphs.text: Among stomatin-deficient cases, Fricke et al. (2004) found that the temperature dependence of the passive K+ leak varied. In 3 cases the leak rose steadily with temperature. In 2 cases the leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C and very high at 0 degrees C, giving the cryohydrocytosis phenotype.

checks.explanation: Directly stated.

checks.claim: In 3 stomatin-deficient cases studied by Fricke et al. (2004), the passive K+ leak rose steadily with temperature.

checks.explanation: A simple monotonic dependence corresponds to a leak that rises steadily with temperature.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that the multisystem disease probably reflects 2 combined effects. The first is deficient glucose transport at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency. The second is the harmful osmotic effect of a cation-leaky membrane protein in cells that express GLUT1, notably the red cell.

checks.evidence_quote: The multisystem pathology probably reflects a combination of glucose transport deficiency at the blood-brain barrier (as in typical GLUT1 deficiency) and the deleterious osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein
checks.explanation: The authors propose two combined mechanisms for the multisystem pathology. They do not use the disease label 'stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis', but the two-effect explanation matches.

checks.claim: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that one effect is deficient glucose transport at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency.

checks.explanation: The first proposed effect is glucose transport deficiency at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency.

checks.claim: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that the other effect is the harmful osmotic effect of a cation-leaky membrane protein in cells that express GLUT1, notably the red cell.
checks.evidence_quote: the deleterious osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein in the cells where GLUT1 is expressed, notably the red cell.
checks.explanation: The second proposed effect is the osmotic damage from a cation-leaky membrane protein in GLUT1-expressing cells, notably the red cell.

paragraphs.text: In an infant with stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects, Bawazir et al. (2012) identified a trinucleotide deletion in the SLC2A1 gene, predicted to remove isoleucine 435 or 436 (I435del) of GLUT1. The infant had pseudohyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, microcephaly, seizures, developmental delay, periventricular calcification, cataracts, and retinal dysfunction. The infant's red cells were extremely leaky and lost potassium in a temperature-dependent manner.
